newsitem.title: FINLAND: ICE HOCKEY-FINNS DREAM OF BEATING CANADA IN FINALS.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-FINNS DREAM OF BEATING CANADA IN FINALS.

text.p: Beating Canada in the ice hockey world championship finals would be a dream come true for host Finland's coach Curt Lindstrom -- and sweet revenge for a string of past humiliations by the Canadians.

But there is a long way from Saturday's opening matches in the championships -- the fifth on Finnish ice -- to the mid-May finals, and Nordic history suggests the home team is more likely to fail than triumph.
Finland have never won a medal when hosting the event. Their best at home was fourth in 1974, and they came fifth in 1982 and 1991.
Neighbouring Sweden have not captured even one of six world titles at any of the eight championships played there.

In hockey-crazy Finland, hopes are high but feelings mixed after less than impressive performances by the Finnish squad in recent friendlies against arch-rivals Sweden and reigning world champions the Czech Republic.
Confidence was partly restored after a resounding 7-1 victory over Russia in the last warm-up game earlier this week.
Commentators warn that excessive expectations may put unbearable strain on the home team, whose players are treated as national heroes -- or traitors.
But Lindstrom still has his sights set on the finals.
"I dream, over and over again, that we beat Canada in the third world chamionship final," he said. That would be on May 14.

The gold medals will be decided for the first time in a best-of-three final. These clashes - the first two are on May 11 and 13 - will be between the two top teams from a final series featuring the top three teams from each of two preliminary round-robin groups.

Both groups are made up of six national teams. Playing in the brand new 13,000-spectator stadium in Helsinki, group A pits Finland, Russia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Germany and France against each other.
Group B, playing in Turku on the southwest coast, comprises Canada, the United States, Sweden, Italy, Latvia and Norway.
Pundits expect the six-team final series to become a contest between Finland, Russia and the Czech Republic from group A and Canada, the United States and Sweden from group B.
Apart from Britain, who won the 1936 Olympic gold, only these six have ever won an ice hockey Olympic or world title.
"It would be a catastrophe if we failed to finish in the top three of our group," Lindstrom said.

The ultimate strength of the top teams will be clear only with the tournament already well under way. Most coaches keep a few berths open for professionals from teams eliminated in the playoffs of the National Hockey League (NHL).
Finnish fans are hungry for more glory after Finland beat Sweden to take their first ever world title in 1995, but financially the tournament is a guaranteed success.
The organisers say they are cautiously predicting a profit of some 20 million markka ($3.9 million) on the 85 million markka turnover, excluding television rights.
The 51 scheduled matches, or 52 if a third final is needed, are expected to draw up to 430,000 paying spectators generating 55 million markka ticket revenue.

Deals with big local sponsors like telecoms group Nokia, oil and chemicals group Neste, insurer Pohjola and bank Postipankki will bring in 15 million markka, and the organisers expect as much again from stadium sales of food, beverages and trinkets.
So far reports show Finns are evenly split over who they most want the home side to beat in the finals, Canada or Sweden. But Lindstrom, a Swede, wants to take Canada.
During his first season as head coach in 1994, Canada beat Finland 5-3 in the Olympic semi-final, and later that spring trounced the Finns on penalties in the world championship final.
And in the quarter-finals in the Vienna world championships last year, Canada defeated then-titleholders Finland 3-1 and sent them home in humiliation before the medal games.
